title: Peony bloom in cross-stitch
subtitle: A fully open peony head in deep pink and cream on 14-count Aida
excerpt: A peony bloom is a 90-by-85 stitch piece on 14-count Aida. The ruffled concentric petals in five pinks and two creams use ten floss colours. The design is the most colour-intensive in the florals sub-category and is suited to a stitcher comfortable with managing several bobbins at once. Finished size is about 16 x 15 cm.
sourceNotes: Original design for Homemade cross-stitch library. Peony motifs appear extensively in East Asian and European embroidery traditions.

Organise all ten colours on bobbins with the DMC code written on each label before starting. The outer ring colour (3350) and the innermost cream (3865) are the anchors for positioning; place both before filling the middle layers.

items.name: 14-count Aida, white or cream
items.substitutions: Pale sage green Aida makes the pinks read warmer

items.name: Hoop or frame
items.qty: 20 cm (8 inch) hoop or a rectangular frame

content.text: Find the centre of the fabric. The chart centre falls in the central stamen cluster (3865). Stitch this area first, a rough oval of about 15 x 12 stitches, to anchor the design.
Work outward in concentric petal rings: 819 (palest pink), 963 (light pink), 3608 (mid pink), 3609, 3804, 3806, 3805, finishing with 3350 (deepest magenta) at the outermost petal edges.
The leaf and stem area at the base is a small block in 522. Stitch this after the flower head is complete.
Add the back-stitch stem in a single strand of 522 where the stem narrows below the sepal.

Wash gently and press face-down. The large stitch count benefits from framing rather than an unpadded hoop, to prevent the hoop ring distorting the outer petal area over time. A white mount and light wood or gold frame suit the palette.

items.symptom: The petal layers look like concentric rings rather than overlapping petals
items.cause: Each shade was worked as a complete band rather than following the irregular petal shapes on the chart.
items.fix: Follow the chart petal shapes rather than stitching in bands. Each petal outline is irregular; working within the outline first, then filling, gives the overlapping effect once all layers are in.

items.symptom: The pink shades blend poorly at the transitions
items.cause: The thread was not separated and recombined before threading, so the strands are twisted unevenly.
items.fix: Strip each pair of strands individually from the skein and recombine before threading. Stripped and recombined strands lie flat and the colours blend smoothly in the transition zones. The difference is visible once the first transition row is worked.

content.text: Once a multi-colour bloom feels comfortable, try a design with fractional stitches at the petal edges. The peony works well with full crosses. A rose or camellia rewards the extra detail.

glossaryTerms.definition: A stiff, evenly-woven cross-stitch fabric with clearly visible squares formed by groups of threads. The default for beginners. Counted in squares per inch: 11ct, 14ct, 16ct, and 18ct are the common counts.

The six-strand embroidery thread used for cross-stitch. Each skein is made of six strands twisted together loosely; the stitcher strips out the number of strands needed for the fabric count (two strands for 14-count Aida) and threads them together.

A solid outline stitch worked in a single strand along the back-stitch layer of the chart. You stitch backwards along the line one stitch at a time, each stitch finishing where the previous one started.
